title: Social Work Basics
summary: An introduction to social work: values and ethics, the helping process and strengths-based practice, communication and casework, child protection and family support, group work and community development, and policy, supervision and self-care.
audience: Prospective social workers, community and youth workers, NGO staff and volunteers

lessons.title: What social work is: values and ethics

body.p: Social work is a practice-based profession and academic discipline that promotes social change and development, social cohesion, and the empowerment and liberation of people. It works with individuals, families, groups and communities facing challenges such as poverty, abuse, illness, disability, addiction, conflict and displacement.

list: Respect for the dignity and worth of every person.
Social justice: challenging discrimination and unfair structures.
Self-determination: supporting people to make their own choices.
Confidentiality, within legal limits such as protecting someone at serious risk.
Integrity and professional competence.

body.p: International social work bodies, such as the International Federation of Social Workers, publish ethical principles, and national councils register practitioners and set codes of conduct. In many African contexts, social workers draw on ubuntu and community traditions of mutual support alongside formal welfare systems.

body.tip: This course introduces social work. Practising as a social worker requires an accredited qualification and registration with your national council.

body.p: Social workers follow a structured but flexible process with clients.

steps: Engagement: build trust, explain your role, respect and listen.
Assessment: gather information about needs, strengths, risks and resources, using tools such as genograms (family trees) and ecomaps (diagrams of relationships with people and services).
Planning: set goals with the client, not for them.
Intervention: counselling, connecting to services, advocacy, practical support, group work or community action.
Evaluation: check whether goals were met.
Termination or referral: end the relationship well or connect the client to ongoing support.

body.p: Instead of focusing only on problems, a strengths-based approach identifies the client's abilities, relationships, culture and community resources, and builds on them. A grandmother caring for grandchildren may lack income but have strong community ties and parenting experience that the plan can use.

body.tip: In every assessment, record at least as many strengths as problems.

body.p: Effective social work depends on communication skills.

list: Active listening: attention, nodding, summarising and reflecting feelings ("It sounds like you feel let down").
Open questions to explore, closed questions to clarify facts.
Empathy: understanding the person's experience without judging.
Non-verbal communication: posture, eye contact and tone, adjusted to cultural norms.
Working with interpreters when needed, rather than relying on family members.
Clear, factual and timely case recording.

body.p: Caseloads can be heavy. A worker with 30 cases who spends 45 minutes a week on each needs 22.5 hours, leaving 17.5 hours of a 40-hour week for travel, recording, meetings and emergencies. Supervisors use such calculations to keep caseloads safe.

body.tip: Write case notes the same day, separating facts ("Mother said…") from your professional assessment.

body.p: Child protection is a central part of social work. Children have rights to protection, provision and participation under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child.

list: Physical abuse: unexplained injuries.
Emotional abuse: constant criticism, rejection or threats.
Sexual abuse and exploitation.
Neglect: lack of food, shelter, health care, supervision or schooling.
Child labour, trafficking and harmful practices such as child marriage.

body.p: Anyone working with children should know the local reporting procedures. Social workers assess risk, plan for safety, and wherever safe, support families to care for children at home, because family-based care is usually best for children. When children cannot stay at home, options include kinship care, foster care and adoption, with institutional care as a last resort.
Parenting programmes, social grants and cash transfers, early childhood services and links to health care strengthen families and prevent harm.

body.tip: Listen to children directly and take what they say seriously; children's views must be considered in decisions about them.

body.p: Social work also works with groups and whole communities.

Support groups (for example for caregivers, people living with HIV or survivors of violence), skills groups and therapeutic groups help members share experience, reduce isolation and learn from each other. A group of 6 meeting weekly for 4 weeks gives 24 attendances of support that a single worker could not provide individually.

list: Identify community needs and assets together with residents.
Build local leadership and organisations.
Mobilise resources and partnerships with government, NGOs and businesses.
Advocate for policy changes, such as better services or access to social grants.
Evaluate projects with community members.

body.p: Participation is essential: projects designed with communities, not merely for them, are more sustainable.

body.tip: Map community assets first: people, groups, places and skills. Communities have more resources than a problem-only view shows.

body.p: Social workers operate within social policies and laws: social grants and pensions, child protection laws, disability services, housing and health policies. Understanding them lets workers connect clients to entitlements and advocate for better policies.

Professional supervision provides support, accountability and learning. Workers discuss difficult cases, check decisions and reflect on their practice. If a district has 120 vulnerable families and each worker can safely support 30, at least 4 workers are needed, a calculation supervisors use when arguing for staffing.

Exposure to trauma and heavy workloads can cause burnout and secondary traumatic stress. Protect your wellbeing through supervision, peer support, boundaries between work and home, rest and seeking counselling when needed. Caring for yourself is part of caring well for others.

body.tip: Notice early signs of burnout, such as exhaustion and detachment, and raise them in supervision rather than waiting.

quiz.q: Which is a core social work value?
options: Respect for the dignity of every person
Supporting people to make their own choices

quiz.q: A diagram of a client's relationships with people and services is a:
Who should set goals in planning?
options: The client together with the worker
Builds on clients' abilities and resources

quiz.q: "It sounds like you feel let down" is an example of:
30 cases at 45 minutes a week each take how many hours?
Which is a sign of neglect?
options: Lack of food, health care or supervision

quiz.q: When children cannot stay at home, the last resort is usually:

options: With communities, not merely for them
